newsitem.title: FRANCE: Far right seeks control in French town election.
newsitem.headline: Far right seeks control in French town election.

text.p: Residents of a southern French town voted on Sunday in a bitterly-contested election with the far-right National Front (FN) seeking to win control of a fourth municipality.

Turnout at midday (1100 GMT) was 35.76 percent, down from 37.88 percent in a 1995 election scrapped because of voting irregularities. Analysts reckon a low turnout would benefit the FN, whose voters are more militant.

The elections in Vitrolles, a mushrooming town of 30,000 people near the port of Marseilles where unemployment is 19 percent, will test the lure of the FN's anti-immigrant policies in the run-up to parliamentary elections in 1998.
The campaign has been marred by court wrangles over alleged dirty tricks and scattered violence.
In the last municipal elections in June 1995, the FN won control of its first three towns -- Toulon, Orange and Marignane, all in southern France.

Socialist mayor Jean-Jacques Anglade won the scrapped 1995 vote in Vitrolles by a scant 353 votes ahead of FN candidate Bruno Megret, a deputy to FN leader Jean-Marie Le Pen who wants to send home three million immigrants.

On Sunday, Megret's wife Catherine is heading the "Allez Vitrolles" (Go Vitrolles) list for the FN against Anglade -- Bruno Megret has been barred from running for exceeding campaign spending limits in 1995.

The candidate for the government's RPR-UDF coalition, Roger Guichard, protested late on Saturday that the Allez Vitrolles list failed to mention the FN and that one of its candidate was even listed as a former RPR-UDF member.
"There is obviously the risk of damaging confusion for the electors of Vitrolles," he said in a statement. If no candidate wins an outright majority, a second round will be held next Sunday.
